Formulation:
Predisposing: Family history of migraine; estrogen-containing OCP.  
Precipitating: Possible hormonal trigger; sudden onset on waking 3 days ago.  
Perpetuating: Ongoing visual sensitivity and inadequate pain control; work disruption increasing distress.  
Protective: Insightful, seeks medical help, able to follow safety advice.

Mental Health Care Plan Details

Principal Problem: Severe persistent headache likely migraine with aura
- Patient Goal(s): Obtain pain relief; resume normal work activities; understand triggers
- Clinical Goal(s): Confirm diagnosis; exclude secondary causes (CVST, IIH); provide effective acute and prophylactic management
- Actions (Patient):
  • Start prescribed stronger NSAID and Paracetamol with food  
  • Maintain headache diary (timing, severity, triggers, medication taken)  
  • Seek urgent care (A&E) if headache worsens, neurological symptoms develop, or pain becomes unbearable
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  • Arrange face-to-face appointment for full neurological and fundoscopic examination and blood-pressure check  
  • Consider neuro-imaging / urgent referral if red-flag findings or high suspicion of secondary cause  
  • Review suitability of current OCP; discuss alternative contraception if migraine with aura confirmed  
  • Provide acute migraine management plan and discuss potential prophylactic options at follow-up

Secondary Problem: Potential OCP-related migraine / hormonal trigger
- Patient Goal(s): Understand relationship between contraception and headaches
- Clinical Goal(s): Evaluate need to change contraceptive method
- Actions (Patient):
  • Continue current OCP until reviewed unless severe aura or neurologic symptoms develop  
  • Note timing of headaches in relation to pill cycle
- Actions (Clinician/GP):
  • Review BP and migraine characteristics; determine if combined OCP contraindicated  
  • Offer alternative non-estrogen contraception if indicated

Patient Education, Emergency Care & Relapse Prevention:
- Education Given: Yes. Topics Covered: Nature of migraine, medication use (NSAID, Paracetamol), red-flag symptoms warranting emergency care, impact of estrogen-containing OCP
- Early Warning Signs of Relapse/Worsening: Escalating pain >8/10, new neurological deficits, visual changes persisting >1 hour, vomiting, inability to control pain with medication
- Coping Strategies: Rest in dark room, hydration, headache diary, scheduled breaks from screen work

Consent, Coordination & Review:
- Patient Consent to Plan: Obtained verbally
- Copy of Mental Health Care Plan Given to Patient: To be sent via patient portal
- Other Mental Health Professionals Involved in Patient Care: None at present
- GP Acknowledgment (if completed by other MH Professional): Not applicable
- Review Date: Within 4 weeks or sooner if symptoms escalate

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)
- Migraine with visual aura – High likelihood: Unilateral severe headache, photophobia, visual phenomena, family history
- Cerebral Venous Sinus Thrombosis – Medium likelihood: Female on estrogen OCP, new persistent headache, positional component
- Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension – Medium likelihood: Young woman with visual disturbance; needs fundoscopic exam

Quality checks
● Missing but clinically expected elements: Comprehensive MSE, formal cognitive assessment, suicide risk assessment, patient demographics, vital signs, medication doses  
● Internal conflicts: None noted between transcript and DDx
